newsitem.title: USA: McVeigh remains stoical as death sentence is read.
newsitem.headline: McVeigh remains stoical as death sentence is read.

text.p: There were only a few gasps in the court when the judge read the chilling words that condemned Timothy McVeigh to death. But not a murmur was heard from the Oklahoma City bomber himself.
The decorated Gulf War veteran sat still and soldier-like without any visible expression, like he has throughout the seven-week trial.
His chief lawyer, Stephen Jones, said McVeigh had expected the death sentence for the April 19, 1995 bombing of the Alfred P. Murrah federal building that killed 168 people.
When the judge excused him from the courtroom, McVeigh, 29, looked at his heart-broken parents and appeared to mouth the words: "It's alright."

The ex-soldier, who grew up in a small western, N.Y., town, then gave a small wave to the jury that voted to send him to his death and nodded to the judge who will formally pronounce that sentence at a hearing next month.
His sister, Jennifer, who testified against him under a grant of immunity from prosecution, cried. His divorced parents sat motionless.
After the short proceeding, members of the defence team hugged the relatives. McVeigh's mother, Mildred Frazer, who lives in Florida, looked lost and weary.
While the death verdict was what most people who lost loved ones in the bombing said they wanted, there were no cheers even after the proceedings were over.
Many, in fact, looked numb. Outside the courtroom prosecutor Vicki Behenna had tears in her eyes as she hugged some of the bombing victims.

"This is not a day of great joy for the prosecution team. We're pleased that the system worked and that justice prevailed. But the verdict doesn't diminish the great sadness that occurred in Oklahoma City two years ago," chief prosecutor Joe Hartzler said.

Hartzler, who has multiple sclerosis and gets around in a motorized wheel chair, was cheered by passersby as he left the courtroom. He was surrounded by security guards and followed for blocks by a hoard of journalists and television cameramen.
Federal Judge Richard Matsch thanked the jurors before excusing them for the last time and warned them to expect to be approached by news people to explain their verdict.
"You may very well find people at your doorstep, you can expect that," Matsch told the jurors. He also told them they did not have to answer to anyone.

Now that the trial is over, jurors are free to talk about their deliberations. But Matsch cautioned them about making remarks about Terry Nichols, McVeigh's alleged co-conspirator who will be tried later this year. While Nichols' name was mentioned during the trial, Matsch noted "he hasn't had a fair trial in front of you."
Legal experts said McVeigh could be executed within three to four years if his sentence is not overturned, although the appeals process will start immediately.
